q: Loans exceeding the deposites means
explanation: When banks' loans exceed their (cash) deposits, the extra is created as new deposits – credit creation.

q: Which of the following are used for measuring the high-power money supply (H) by RBI in India?
options: Currency held by the public + Other deposits with the RBI
Cash reserves of the commercial banks + Other deposits with the RBI

notes.text: - **H = currency held by the public + cash reserves of banks (with themselves and with RBI) + other deposits with RBI**; no time deposits, no post-office deposits, no forex held by persons.

explanation: High-powered money (reserve money) is M0 — currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with the RBI + other deposits with the RBI. The option printed 'Mx' is a misprint of M0. M2, M3 and M4 are broader money measures, not reserve money.

notes.text: - Names: **reserve money, monetary base, base money, central bank money** = **M0** – the "most important indicator"; **basis of credit creation**.
> High-powered money = M0, not M2 (an old APPSC key gave M2).

q: Expand the abbreviation 'CRR' used by Reserve Bank of India which all Indian banks must adhere to:
explanation: CRR = Cash Reserve Ratio, the share of NDTL every bank must keep as cash with the RBI; the other expansions are not real terms.

notes.text: - **CRR = Cash Reserve Ratio:** the share of a bank's **Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)** that it must keep as **cash balances with the RBI** (CDS 2020; APPSC AEE 2008).

q: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) according to the recent RBI review (2019) is
explanation:
SLR fell in 25-bps steps through 2019-20 — now 18% of NDTL since 11 April 2020 (RBI notification, 5 Dec 2018)
Under the December 2018 review the SLR was cut by 25 bps a quarter, to 19.25% from 5 January 2019 (then 19.0% April, 18.75% July 2019) (now 18% since April 2020).

q: If the cash reserve ratio is lowered by the RBI credit creation will
explanation: A lower CRR leaves banks more lendable funds and raises the money multiplier, so credit creation increases.

notes.text: - **Lowering CRR:** **credit creation increases** (APPSC G2 2017); banks get **higher leverage to liquidity** and the economy **may see increased investment** (NextGen: lower CRR "helps banks provide loans … for investment purposes" and "boosts the growth rate").

q:
Statutory Liquidity Ratio is to be maintained by banks in the form of

I. Cash.

II. Gold.

III. Unencumbered investments in specified instruments

IV. Priority sector loans
explanation: SLR assets are cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities (G-secs, T-bills); priority-sector loans are lending, not SLR assets, so I, II and III.

notes.text: - **SLR:** minimum share of NDTL a bank keeps **with itself** in liquid assets **before lending** – **cash, gold and unencumbered approved/Government securities (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs)**; **not priority-sector loans** (APPSC G1 2023: I, II and III).

q: The cash reserve ratio of Commercial Banks in India is determined by
explanation: The CRR is fixed by the central bank (RBI) under Section 42 of the RBI Act, not by the Finance Ministry, the market or the BoP.

q: Which of the following is CORRECT regarding the term ‘Required Reserve Ratio’?

Percentage of reserves a company should keep to maintain its supply stock

q:
When the Central Bank increases the Cash Reserve Ratio, it leads to
I. Fall in money circulation.
II. Low demand for goods and services.
III. Rise in purchasing power of the people. 63
IV. Rise in bank's lending capacity.
explanation: A CRR hike leaves banks less to lend, so money in circulation falls and demand for goods and services falls; purchasing power and lending capacity do not rise, so I and II only.

q: Repo rates are money market instruments which are used
options: to regulate liquidity in the economy
to help the government to meet to short-term credit needs
key_text: to regulate liquidity in the economy
explanation: Repo is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against G-secs; it is used to inject or withdraw liquidity and so regulate liquidity in the economy, not to curb black money or fund the Government.

notes.text: - **Rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks / at which banks borrow from RBI = Repo rate** (UPPSC 2005, 2008, 2013; SI 2019; APPSC G2; AP recruitment); comes under **monetary policy**; used **to regulate liquidity** (APPSC G2 2017).

q: How does the introduction of the Standing Deposit (4) Facility (SDF) enhance the RBI's liquidity management framework?
options: By increasing overall liquidity in the banking system far und Dis
By absorbing surplus liquidity without the need for collateral
By keeping the cost of liquidity for commercial banks constant
By providing long-term loans to banks at lower interest rates
key_text: By absorbing surplus liquidity without the need for collateral
explanation: The SDF (April 2022) lets the RBI absorb surplus liquidity without giving G-secs as collateral, unlike the reverse repo; it absorbs, so it does not add liquidity or give long-term loans.

notes.text: - **SDF** (proposed 2015, enabled by **Budget 2018-19**, began **April 2022**): absorbs surplus liquidity **without collateral** – the only collateral-free absorption tool (APPSC G2).

q: Repo Rate is the rate at which

RBI borrows money from the commercial banks
RBI lends money to the capital market
RBI borrows money from the capital market

explanation: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks against G-secs; RBI borrowing from banks is the reverse repo.

notes.text: - **Rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks / at which banks borrow from RBI = Repo rate** (UPPSC 2005, 2008, 2013; SI 2019; APPSC G2; AP recruitment); comes under **monetary policy**; used **to regulate liquidity** (APPSC G2 2017).

q: What is the means of borrowing money by commercial banks through repurchase agreements (REPOs)?
explanation: Under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility banks borrow from the RBI through repurchase agreements (repos) and lend through reverse repos; the bank rate has no collateral repo.

notes.text: - **LAF (June 2000):** the window through which banks **borrow via repos** and **lend via reverse repos** – "borrowing through repurchase agreements" = **LAF** (APPSC G2).

explanation: The MSF (May 2011) was created to contain volatility in the overnight inter-bank rate by letting banks borrow overnight above repo; LAF is the general repo window and MSS absorbs forex-linked liquidity.

III. 'Tenor Premium' is an important component in the calculation of the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR).

IV. Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is used as a long-term policy rate and is generally lower than the Bank Rate.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
explanation: I is wrong (a CRR hike reduces credit creation); II is wrong (CRR applies to all NDTL and the I-CRR to the incremental deposit base, not borrowers); III is right (tenor premium is an MCLR component); IV is wrong (MSF is overnight and equals the Bank Rate). Only III.

notes.text: - **APPSC G1 2024 statements:** CRR hike **reduces** credit creation (I ✗); I-CRR targeted **incremental deposits**, not borrowers (II ✗); **tenor premium is an MCLR component** (III ✓); MSF is an **overnight** rate **equal to** Bank Rate, not long-term or lower (IV ✗) → **only III**.
